content.description: Thinking, a heartbeat, lifting an arm: all of it travels first as living electricity, carried not by electrons but by ions.

hero.hook: Your body is an electrical network. Only here the current is made of ions, not electrons.

blocks.text: In a wall socket, the current is a flow of **electrons**. In your body it works differently: **ions**, atoms that carry a charge, move in and out of the cells. That flow creates the signals that let you think, keep your heart beating, and make a muscle contract.
Without this living electricity there would be no thought, no movement, no pulse. Understanding the body also means understanding this language of charges.

A **neuron** at rest sends no message, but it does “charge up.” Its membrane separates the inside of the cell from the outside. Thanks to its [[sodium-potassium pumps]], it holds a [[resting potential]] of about **-70 millivolts**: the inside is more negative than the outside.

blocks.caption: Neurons talk to each other in brief electrical pulses

blocks.text: When a stimulus arrives, channels open. Sodium rushes in. The polarity flips, and that is the [[action potential]], an all-or-nothing signal that races along the axon, sometimes for a full meter. Like an electrical wave.
An awake brain runs on about **20 watts**, enough for a small LED. Even so, it burns close to **20%** of the body's calories.

sections.title: The electric click of a neuron

blocks.text: Neurons do not really touch. Between them lies a tiny gap: the **synapse**. The electrical signal cannot jump it. So the tip of the axon releases [[neurotransmitters]], messenger molecules such as acetylcholine or [[glutamate]].
These messengers fit onto the next neuron like a key in a lock. Depending on the message, they either excite it or hold it back. Thousands of these decisions at once add up to thought.
Some nerve signals travel at **120 m/s**, more than **430 km/h**. Fast enough to react to a burn on your toe in a fraction of a second.

sections.title: At the synapse, electricity turns into chemistry

blocks.text: The heart does not wait for an order from the brain for every beat. In the right atrium, the **sinus node** generates its own pulses, about **60 to 100** times a minute at rest. The signal spreads out, squeezing the atria first, then the ventricles.

This activity is strong enough to be read from the skin, which is what an **electrocardiogram (ECG)** does. When the rhythm goes wrong, doctors call it an **arrhythmia**. The heart then beats out of order and pumps badly.
The electric eel uses the same excitable cells, only wired in series: up to **600 volts**, enough to paralyze its prey.

sections.title: The heart has its own pacemaker

blocks.text: To lift your arm, an action potential runs down to the muscle. Acetylcholine sets off a local electrical wave, then a release of calcium. The muscle proteins slide over one another, and that is the contraction.

**Defibrillation** uses the same principle in reverse: a shock from outside resets every cell “to zero” so the sinus node can take the tempo back. Bionic limbs also pick up these faint signals to drive an artificial hand.
Living bodies speak in flows of ions and action potentials. Thought, heart, and muscle all share the same electrical language.

sections.title: From a lifted arm to the defibrillator

American shale oil revolution.explanation: Massive boom in American production in the 21st century thanks to hydraulic fracturing, modifying the world's geopolitical energy balance.

Hippocampus.explanation: Sea-horse-shaped brain structure in the temporal lobe, essential for the formation of new conscious memories. Its surgical removal (case H.M.) leads to a total inability to form new memories, without erasing old ones.

Neurotransmitters.explanation: Chemical molecules released in the synapse that transmit the signal between neurons. The main ones: glutamate (excitatory), GABA (inhibitory), dopamine, serotonin. Psychoactive drugs act on these systems.

Oil futures market.explanation: Contracts by which buyers and sellers commit to a future transaction at a price fixed today. Speculators with no intention of physical delivery represent the vast majority of transactions, amplifying price fluctuations.

The neuronal action potential.explanation: An all-or-nothing electrical signal triggered when the depolarization of a neuron exceeds a threshold. It propagates along the axon at 1 to 100 m/s depending on myelination. It is the "click" of information that the neuron sends.

Working memory.explanation: Cognitive system that temporarily maintains a small amount of information (7±2 items) available for current processing. Managed by the prefrontal cortex, it is limited in capacity and duration (a few seconds without repetition).

action potential.explanation: An all-or-nothing electrical signal triggered when the depolarization of a neuron exceeds a threshold. It propagates along the axon at 1 to 100 m/s depending on myelination. It is the "click" of information that the neuron sends.

glutamate.explanation: The primary excitatory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system, playing a crucial role in neuronal plasticity and memory.

neuronal action potential.explanation: An all-or-nothing electrical signal triggered when the depolarization of a neuron exceeds a threshold. It propagates along the axon at 1 to 100 m/s depending on myelination. It is the "click" of information that the neuron sends.

neurotransmitters.explanation: Chemical molecules released in the synapse that transmit the signal between neurons. The main ones: glutamate (excitatory), GABA (inhibitory), dopamine, serotonin. Psychoactive drugs act on these systems.

resting potential.explanation: Stable state of the electrical voltage across a neuron's membrane when it is not transmitting a signal (approximately -70 millivolts).

sodium-potassium pumps.explanation: Membrane proteins that use cellular energy (ATP) to maintain the ionic concentration gradients necessary for the resting potential.

quiz.explanation: In a wall outlet, electrons circulate; in the body, these are ions, charged atoms, which enter and leave cells.
options: Ions, charged atoms that move in and out of cells
Free electrons circulating in the blood
Magnetic waves produced by the brain
Static electricity accumulated in the skin
quiz.question: In the body, what circulates to create electrical signals, unlike a wall outlet?

quiz.explanation: Thanks to sodium-potassium pumps, a neuron at rest maintains a potential of around -70 millivolts, with the inside being more negative than the outside.
quiz.question: Approximately what is the resting potential of a neuron, in millivolts?

quiz.explanation: When a stimulus arrives, sodium rushes in and the polarity flips: that's the action potential, an all-or-nothing signal that runs down the axon.
options: An all-or-nothing electrical signal that runs along the axon when sodium suddenly enters
The level of energy the neuron consumes at rest
The amount of neurotransmitters stored in the neuron
The time it takes for a neuron to regenerate after use
quiz.question: What is the action potential of a neuron?

quiz.explanation: The electrical signal cannot jump the synapse: the axon releases neurotransmitters which attach to the next neuron like a key in a lock.
options: By releasing neurotransmitters which attach to the next neuron
By directly sending an electric current through space
By temporarily fusing its membrane with that of the next neuron
By releasing calcium ions which pass through space freely
quiz.question: How does a neuron transmit its signal across the synapse, the space that separates it from the next neuron?

quiz.explanation: Some nerve signals travel at around 120 m/s, or more than 430 km/h, enough to respond almost instantly to a burn.
quiz.question: Approximately how fast do certain nerve signals travel, in meters per second?

quiz.explanation: In the right atrium, the sinus node generates its own electrical impulses, approximately 60 to 100 times per minute at rest.
options: The structure that itself generates the electrical impulses of the heartbeat
The valve that separates the atria from the ventricles
The main muscle that pumps blood to the lungs
The nerve that connects the heart directly to the brain
quiz.question: What is the sinus node in the heart?

quiz.explanation: The heart does not wait for an order from the brain for each beat: the sinus node itself generates its own electrical impulses.
options: True
False
quiz.question: True or false: the heart needs a command from the brain for each beat.

quiz.explanation: The electric eel uses the same principle of excitable cells as the human body, but in series, up to 600 volts, enough to paralyze prey.
quiz.question: How many volts can an electric eel produce?

quiz.explanation: Defibrillation sends an external shock that resets all cardiac cells, so that the sinus node returns to normal tempo.
options: It sends a shock which resets all the cardiac cells so that the sinus node resumes the tempo
It directly stimulates the brain to revive the heart
It chemically replaces the heartbeat with a permanent artificial rhythm
It completely blocks the electrical activity of the heart
quiz.question: What does defibrillation do?
